investigation.title: Remote Agents: Swarm Gateway 502 Blocking All Agent Provisioning Evals
investigation.summary: All three remote-agents checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed at 2026-09-19T12:32 with an identical 502 bad_gateway error indicating the swarm gateway ELB endpoint at /v1/agents was unreachable during agent provisioning. Because the failure occurs at the POST /api/agents boundary before any agent identity or VM data is returned, all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) are absent and every contract assertion is unverifiable.
investigation.rootCause: The swarm gateway — the AWS ELB-backed upstream service reached via POST to /v1/agents — was unreachable at the time of the eval run. The production-api layer returned HTTP 502 with code "bad_gateway" and the message "error sending request for url (http://[REDACTED].elb.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/v1/agents)", meaning the connection to the ELB either timed out or was refused before any agent provisioning could begin. This is an infrastructure-layer failure localized to the swarm gateway dependency, not to the eval runner logic itself. No user-traffic or incident signals are present in the supplied evidence, so impact is confirmed only at the eval observability layer.

possibleCauses: Primary: The swarm gateway ELB (us-east-2) was down, misconfigured, or had no healthy targets at the time of the eval run, causing the production-api to receive a connection error and surface it as a 502 bad_gateway.
Secondary: A network-level routing or security-group change between the production-api and the swarm ELB blocked outbound connections to the /v1/agents endpoint, producing the same 502 symptom.

Tertiary: The swarm gateway service itself was in a crash loop or was being redeployed at the time of the eval run, causing transient unavailability that resolved before or after the ~34-second window spanning all three checks.
Lower probability: The ELB DNS name was changed or deregistered, causing DNS resolution to fail or route to an unreachable address, which the production-api surfaces as a bad_gateway error.

If a subsequent eval run shows snapshotAgeMinutes <= 300 without any workflow changes, it would suggest the failure was a transient scheduling gap rather than a persistent workflow breakage.
If the snapshot URL returns a 404 or non-JSON response, the root cause would shift from staleness to a publication or hosting failure rather than a missed workflow run.

If the snapshotAgeMinutes value computed by statusSnapshotEvidence is shown to be derived from a field other than the snapshot's actual generation timestamp (e.g., a cached or default value), the staleness signal would be unreliable and the diagnosis would need revision.
